title: Undertow and Language
premise: Xanthe Yarrow, a piano tuner who reads a house's history through its pipes and radiators, is hired to tune the piano at the Holloway estate on the day of the family matriarch's funeral. There he meets a stranger who calls the dead woman by her childhood name — a name no living relative uses — and Xanthe realizes the man, Elias, is the son she gave up decades ago to protect the family's standing. As Xanthe is drawn into the household's web of silence, he becomes the unlikely translator between a family that communicates only in duty and a brother they never knew they had. The story ends with Xanthe forcing the eldest son, Marcus, to speak the unsaid aloud at last; Elias leaves with the truth acknowledged if not forgiven, and Xanthe, having finally said his own goodbye to the father he never mourned properly, walks out of the house with its radiators gone quiet behind him.
about_author: O. M. Thackeray spent fifteen years as a building conservator in coastal towns before turning to fiction, and still claims old houses talk if you press your ear to the right pipe. Undertow and Language is their third novel, following two quietly acclaimed books about inheritance, work, and the things families refuse to say.

chapters.title: The Tuner's Ear
chapters.summary: POV: Xanthe. Arriving at the Holloway estate to tune the piano for a funeral reception, Xanthe maps the house through its plumbing — grief in the radiators, secrets in the basement pipes. He notices the family speaks in logistics, never feelings. Emotional beat: quiet unease; a professional observer recognizing a household built entirely out of things unsaid.

chapters.title: A Name Nobody Uses
chapters.summary: POV: Xanthe. At the wake, a weathered stranger appears at the edge of the garden, and the matriarch's sister goes white when he says 'hello, Nell.' Xanthe watches the family close ranks around him like water around a stone. Emotional beat: intrusion; the first crack in the family's careful surface, and Xanthe's reluctant curiosity ignited.

chapters.title: Inventory of Unsaid Things
chapters.summary: POV: Xanthe. Asked to stay and service the house's ancient boiler, Xanthe begins keeping his private ledger of silences: the portrait turned to the wall, the locked room, the way Marcus corrects anyone who mentions 1974. Emotional beat: complicity deepening; Xanthe realizes he is being kept not for his tools but as a neutral witness.

chapters.title: Elias
chapters.summary: POV: alternating Xanthe and Elias. Elias tells Xanthe, over cheap whisky in the boathouse, that Nell was his mother — that he found letters after the man who raised him died. He doesn't want money or apology; he wants one honest conversation. Emotional beat: raw hope meeting guarded sympathy; two outsiders recognize each other.

chapters.title: What the House Keeps
chapters.summary: POV: Xanthe. Working in the walls, Xanthe finds evidence of the secret's cost: a second set of baby records, a doctor's bill from a coastal town, payments stopped abruptly in 1975. He confronts the aunt, Vivian, who reveals Nell gave Elias up under pressure from her husband to protect an inheritance. Emotional beat: revelation; power shown corrupting love into paperwork.

chapters.title: Marcus
chapters.summary: POV: Marcus. The eldest son, executor of the will and keeper of the family's dignity, discovers Xanthe has been talking to Elias. His chapters of controlled grief fracture — he knew, vaguely, always, and built his whole life on never knowing. Emotional beat: rising tension; duty revealed as its own kind of cowardice, and Marcus begins watching Xanthe as a threat.

chapters.title: Undertow
chapters.summary: POV: Xanthe. Marcus dismisses Xanthe and has Elias escorted off the property; the confrontation turns physical and humiliating. That night Xanthe hears the house's pipes groaning like something drowning, and understands he must choose between safe silence and speaking. Emotional beat: crisis of conscience; the low point where belonging is offered at the price of complicity.

chapters.title: The Reading
chapters.summary: POV: Xanthe. At the will reading, Marcus announces the estate passes intact to him and Vivian, erasing even a token bequest to charity Nell loved. Xanthe, uninvited but present to collect his tools, watches the family perform gratitude. Emotional beat: tightening screw; injustice done politely, setting the stage for rupture.

chapters.title: Out Loud
chapters.summary: POV: Xanthe and Marcus. On his last morning, Xanthe plays the tuned piano — Nell's own piece — and refuses to leave until Marcus says it: that his mother had another son, that she grieved, that the family chose money over her. Marcus finally speaks the words aloud, shaking, while Elias listens from the doorway. Emotional beat: climax; language breaking the undertow at last.

chapters.title: Gone Quiet
chapters.summary: POV: Xanthe. Weeks later, Elias writes to Xanthe: no reconciliation yet, but Marcus sends photographs, and the locked room stands open. Xanthe visits his father's grave and says his own long-delayed goodbye aloud. Emotional beat: resolution; imperfect, unfinished forgiveness — and a tuner leaving a house whose pipes, for once, have nothing left to tell him.
